doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

chapter: Growing up with his father's music
title: His father, a bassist and his first teacher
summary: He explains he is the second bass player in the family and recalls his father emulating Slam Stewart and playing in a duo called The Rollers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: It would be an eye opener. Well let me ask you about your process of gaining wisdom. I understand you come from a two bass family?
Well a one bass family. I mean well I’m the second bass. My father was a bass player and he was my teacher.
Do you have an early — what’s your earliest recollection of your father playing gigs?

My earliest recollection of my father playing the bass is when I was a little boy. He used to sit on the sofa and put the bass between his legs and bow. One of his favorites was Slam Stewart. And my father — and Slam Stewart always had this, he developed this great bowing style, singing, the same phrases that he would play. And my father used to emulate that. And he was a great musician. He played piano and he also played drums. And so he was always playing music around the house. There was records, his musicians would come over to the house and they’d rehearse. Once he had a duo, he and a piano player, they were working together as a duo. They’d play all these different gigs. They were called The Rollers. Kenny Andrews was his name. Kenny Andrews would come over and he and my father would practice and I’d sit there and I’d listen to them, and they used to sing, play and sing. And then when I was about 16 or 17, my father used to start taking me out on gigs with him. And he would play drums and I would play the bass. So that was my earliest recollection of — well of course when I was a kid I’d see him leaving out on gigs, I used to run behind his car sometimes. He’s leaving out on the road, you know — “Daddy, Daddy, Daddy.” I remember one time running behind his car and my father was heartbroken because he had to go away. So very early on.
